title: Undo and redo with two stacks

blocks.text: The page's invoker keeps **two stacks**: executed commands on the undo stack, undone commands on the redo stack. Its critical rule: **a new command clears the redo stack**, or redo would replay a history that no longer exists. It also advises a size limit, because an unbounded undo stack keeps growing.

items: `new CommandHistory(limit)` keeps at most `limit` commands to undo (`limit < 1` throws `IllegalArgumentException`). When a new command would go past the limit, **the oldest one is dropped**.
`executeCommand(c)` runs `c`, pushes it on the undo stack and clears the redo stack (`null` throws `IllegalArgumentException`).

`undo()` pops the newest command, undoes it and pushes it on the redo stack; `redo()` pops from the redo stack, executes it again and pushes it back on the undo stack. **With nothing to undo (or redo), they return `false`**; otherwise `true`.
`canUndo()`, `canRedo()`, `undoSize()`, `redoSize()`, and `getUndoHistory()`: the descriptions on the undo stack, **newest first**.

headers: calls (each command adds its number to a total)

cases.says: Executed commands can be undone newest first and redone in turn; undo() and redo() return true when they did something.
After an undo, executing a new command leaves nothing to redo: redo() returns false and changes nothing.
undo() on an empty history returns false instead of throwing, and redo() likewise.
getUndoHistory() lists the descriptions from the most recent command to the oldest.
With a limit of 2, a third command pushes out the oldest, so the two newest can still be undone.

concepts: An undo history has a maximum size and discards the oldest commands when it is full.
Executing a new command clears the redo stack, so redo never replays a history that no longer exists.
The invoker only knows the Command interface, never the concrete command or its receiver.
An invoker implements undo and redo with two stacks, moving a command from one to the other, and reports an empty stack instead of failing.
